pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Pick two renames you made in the exercise. For each, name the criterion that justifies it — and explain why `k` in the sorting loop did NOT need renaming.
expected_points: criteria named explicitly: intent-revealing, not disinformative, one word per concept, distinct/searchable
scope-length rule: a name's length should match how far readers can be from its declaration
k is fine because its scope is a few lines with the declaration in sight; t/mn/x were wide-scope and carried real load

questions.prompt: When should a long function be split, and when does splitting make code worse? Give one concrete example of each.
expected_points: split when multiple abstraction levels or reasons to change mix — e.g. DoData doing parsing, aggregating, and formatting (section comments are the confession)
don't split a cohesive single idea — e.g. carving a binary search into fragments that can't be understood alone
over-splitting signs: once-called helpers whose names restate their bodies, parameter/state threading between fragments
the test is number of reasons to change, not line count

questions.prompt: What does 'a single reason to change' mean? Which reasons to change were tangled in the original DoData, and how does your refactored version separate them?
expected_points: a reason to change is a requirement-shaped force: input format, statistics rules, output layout
the original mixed all three, so any change risked and required re-reading the others
after the split each function owns one force: parse / summarize / format, with data flowing via parameters and results

questions.prompt: What must a comment do to earn its place? Classify these from the exercise: `// loop over the lines`, the trailing-newline comment on the blank-line skip, the commented-out old DoData, and your new doc comment on the exported function.
expected_points: a comment must say something the code cannot; justified kinds are why, warning, contract
`// loop over the lines` is narration — delete; the urge to narrate signals a rename/extract instead
the trailing-newline comment is a why — keep; commented-out code is dead — version control remembers it
the doc comment is a contract: starts with the name, states edge-case behavior callers rely on, not a signature echo

questions.prompt: You open an unfamiliar 80-line function in a codebase you just joined. Walk me through how you critique it and how you'd order the cleanup — what comes first and why?
expected_points: check names against the criteria, count reasons to change for size/cohesion, triage comments for narration vs why/warning/contract
a prioritized plan with a rationale, e.g. pin behavior with a test first, then safe renames, then structural splits
order justified by risk and by which fixes make later fixes easier

questions.prompt: The starter code was already gofmt-clean, yet it was the worst code in the lesson. What can a formatter fix, and what can it never fix?
expected_points: formatters fix layout: indentation, spacing, uniformity
they cannot fix meaning: names, cohesion, comment quality survive formatting untouched
uniform is not the same as clean

questions.prompt: The exercise tests passed before you changed anything. What were they for, and why was editing their expected output forbidden?
expected_points: characterization tests pin current observable behavior as a refactoring safety net
a refactor preserves behavior by definition, so expected outputs are the fixed point
renaming call sites in tests is part of a rename; changing expectations means you changed behavior, not structure
